A. What action is the EPA taking?
The EPA is fully approving the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality's (ADEQ's) May 30, 2025, SIP revision for MCAQD Rule 205, “Emission Offsets Generated by Voluntary Mobile Source Emission Reductions,” revised on May 21, 2025 (“Rule 205” or “MCAQD Rule 205 submittal”). Specifically, the EPA is approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal by adding Rule 205 into the federally enforceable portion of the Maricopa County portion of the Arizona SIP.[1] Rule 205 allows for the generation of ERCs through voluntary on-road mobile source emissions reductions. ERCs generated by this rule are intended to be used to offset emissions increases of oxides of nitrogen (NOX) and volatile organic compounds (VOC) at major stationary sources as part of the preconstruction permit process required by the CAA's NNSR program.
B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?
We are taking this action under CAA section 110. Pursuant to CAA section 110(a), States are required to submit SIPs to the EPA that provide for the implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of the national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS). CAA section 110(k) requires SIPs to meet certain procedural requirements and requires the EPA to approve or disapprove SIP submissions. CAA section 110(l) requires States to provide public notice and an opportunity for public hearing of SIP revisions prior to their submittal and prohibits the EPA from approving any SIP revisions that would interfere with attainment or maintenance of a NAAQS, reasonable further progress, or other CAA applicable requirements. If a SIP submittal meets all the applicable CAA requirements, then the EPA must approve the submittal under CAA section 110(k)(3).
In evaluating the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal, the EPA considered whether ERCs generated under the rule would meet the statutory and regulatory requirements for offsetting emissions reductions in CAA section 173 and 40 CFR 51.165, respectively. Emissions reductions may generally be credited for NNSR offset purposes under the CAA if they achieve actual emission reductions in the relevant nonattainment area that (1) are not otherwise required by the CAA or relied upon in any air quality-related programs under the CAA; (2) can be reliably quantified using methods that can be replicated; (3) will continue for the duration of the SIP or other program that relies upon the emission reductions; and (4) are enforceable by the EPA under the CAA.
The MCAQD is the local air pollution control agency for Maricopa County, Arizona and is responsible for regulating stationary sources of air pollution within its boundaries. Portions of Maricopa County designated nonattainment for the 2008 and 2015 ozone NAAQS are classified as “Moderate” and portions of Maricopa County designated nonattainment for the 1987 particulate matter 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter (PM10 ) NAAQS are classified as “Serious.” [2] In these nonattainment areas, the MCAQD is required to implement an NNSR permit program for preconstruction review of new or modified major stationary sources.[3] One of the requirements of the NNSR program is to provide surplus emissions reductions to offset a proposed project's projected emissions increases.[4]
The MCAQD has stated that the quantity of surplus emissions reductions currently available for use as NNSR offsets do not appear sufficient to support current and projected economic growth. To incentivize the generation of additional offsets, the MCAQD developed Rule 205 to create a regulatory structure for the generation and use of NOX and VOC ERCs from a nontraditional category. Rule 205 can be used to generate NOX and VOC ERCs from on-road mobile sources, or mobile source ERCs (MERCs). The rule allows ( printed page 69696) on-road mobile source fleet owners/operators that permanently reduce NOX or VOC emissions from their fleets, or credit “generators,” to trade those reductions with stationary sources, or “credit users,” who can then use them to offset their proposed NOX or VOC emissions increases for the purpose of meeting NNSR permit requirements.
On April 16, 2026, the EPA proposed approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal because we determined that this SIP revision complied with all relevant CAA requirements.[5] Table 1 lists the materials we are incorporating into the Arizona SIP. The proposed action and technical support document (TSD) contain more information on the submittal and our evaluation.

III. Public Comments and EPA Responses
The EPA provided a 30-day public comment period on our proposed action. The comment period opened on April 16, 2026, the date of publication in the Federal Register , and closed on May 18, 2026.[6] During this period, the EPA received comments from five separate commenters. All comments submitted during the public comment period can be found in the docket of this rulemaking.[7]
Four commenters were supportive of the EPA's proposed action.[8] In addition to support for the proposed action, two of these commenters included additional recommendations for the EPA to consider. One commenter recommended that the EPA: (1) clarify that “future MCAQD revisions incorporating technology-neutral language for software/operational reductions” would be approvable if the offset integrity criteria are satisfied and (2) commit to updating EPA's Economic Incentive Program (EIP) guidance to clarify that “software-driven mobile source reductions can qualify for MERCs/NNSR offsets when properly documented and enforced.” Another commenter encouraged the EPA to continue to take actions that will encourage the generation of ERCs, improve the efficiency of the ERC certification process, and focus on practical actions that could meaningfully improve public health and reduce air pollution. These recommendations from commenters are outside the scope of our final action on the Department's submittal.
One commenter opposed the EPA's proposed action and requested that the EPA disapprove Rule 205. Below, we summarize the commenter's concerns and provide a response to each.
Comment 1: The commenter asserted that the CAA “does not authorize stationary sources to trade credits with mobile sources because such reductions are not `permanent, quantifiable, and enforceable' as [CAA section] 173(c)(1) requires.” Additionally, the commenter stated Congress separated the authority to regulate stationary sources and mobile sources with no references to linking together with respect to generating offsets.
Response 1: The EPA disagrees with the commenter's claim that mobile source emissions reductions cannot be used as offsets for stationary sources under CAA section 173(c)(1). CAA section 173(a) conditions the issuance of an NNSR permit on a determination by the permitting agency that, among other things, sufficient offsetting emissions reductions will be obtained before the new or modified source commences operation so as to represent “reasonable further progress” toward attainment of the NAAQS.[9] The required offsetting emissions reductions must be in effect and enforceable by the time the new or modified source commences operations and must assure that the total tonnage of increased emissions of the relevant air pollutant from the source is offset by an equal or greater reduction, as applicable, in the actual emissions of that air pollutant in the area.[10] Under CAA section 173(c)(1), ERCs must be obtained from the same source or other sources in the same nonattainment area, except that the reductions may be obtained from another nonattainment area if two conditions are met: (1) the other area has an equal or higher nonattainment classification than the area where the source is located, and (2) emissions from such other area contribute to a violation of the NAAQS in the nonattainment area where the source is located.[11] These restrictions are designed to ensure that offsets result in the improvement of air quality in the nonattainment area, such that construction (or modification) of the source is consistent with reasonable further progress toward attainment.[12]
Consistent with these statutory requirements, the EPA's NNSR implementing regulations require that all emissions reductions claimed as offset credit be “federally enforceable” and that offsetting emissions reductions be obtained from the same source or other sources in the same nonattainment area, except that the reductions may be obtained from another nonattainment area if the two conditions specified in CAA section 173(c)(1) are met.[13] Additionally, the EPA's NNSR regulations provide that emissions reductions achieved by shutting down an existing emission unit or curtailing production or operating hours may be credited for offsets only if, among other things, the reductions are surplus, permanent, quantifiable, and federally ( printed page 69697) enforceable.[14] The EPA has referred to these four creditability criteria in longstanding guidance as “integrity elements”— i.e., elements of a program that ensure it has integrity and meets applicable statutory requirements.[15] The EPA sometimes refers to these integrity elements, along with the requirement in CAA section 173(c)(1) that offsets be based on the reduction of “actual” emissions of the relevant pollutant, as the offset “integrity criteria.” [16]
To the extent the commenter intended to assert that stationary sources are regulated under title I of the CAA while mobile sources are regulated under title II of the CAA, this is generally correct. But nothing in CAA section 173 or any other provision of the CAA prohibits the use of emissions reductions from mobile sources within the relevant nonattainment area for NNSR offset purposes, provided the applicable statutory and regulatory requirements are met. The commenter fails to identify any such prohibition in the text of the CAA or the EPA's implementing regulations. The commenter also fails to support its claim that mobile source emissions reductions would not meet the permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable offset integrity criteria.[17] The EPA's proposed rule and TSD explained in detail how Rule 205 meets the applicable CAA requirements and addresses the EPA's longstanding integrity criteria for offsetting emissions reductions. In the next few paragraphs, we briefly summarize our prior analysis of the permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable criteria.
To ensure emissions reductions from mobile sources meet the permanent criterion, generators of MERCs must demonstrate that replaced vehicles no longer operate in the nonattainment area (NAA) and/or that emissions do not shift to higher emitting vehicles within the fleet. Generators of MERCs do so through enforceable requirements, including robust monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. Rule 205 contains several enforceable conditions to ensure that emissions reductions are permanent, including: limiting the applicability of the rule to “captive fleet” [18] vehicles; requiring the original baseline vehicle to be permanently removed from the Maricopa NAA or rendered permanently disabled and disposed of; [19] requiring any future replacement of the new or retrofitted fleet vehicle to be with a vehicle that is certified to the same or lower emission standard; [20] and related monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements.[21 22]
To ensure emissions reductions from mobile sources meet the quantifiable criterion, generators of MERCs calculate emissions reductions using specific methodologies that are clear and replicable. Appendix A of Rule 205 articulates the calculation formula that MERC generators will use to determine the number of eligible MERCs.[23] Rule 205 requires MERC generators to submit information, within their MERC application, on the methodology for quantifying emissions reductions, including emissions calculations and documentation of each original vehicle's historic vehicle miles traveled.[24 25] Rule 205 also requires MERC generators to demonstrate that the captive fleet of vehicles used to generate MERCs are based and operated within the NAA.[26] Finally, Rule 205 requires the MCAQD to evaluate whether the proposed qualifying emission reductions within the application for MERCs will result in quantifiable emission reductions.[27 28]
To meet the requirement in 40 CFR 51.165(a)(3)(ii)(E) that offsetting emissions reductions be federally enforceable, emissions reductions must be enforceable by the EPA and must be legally and practicably enforceable. The term “federally enforceable” is defined in the EPA's regulations at 40 CFR 51.165(a)(1)(xiv) to mean “all limitations and conditions which are enforceable by the Administrator,” including those requirements developed pursuant to 40 CFR parts 60 and 61, requirements within any applicable SIP, and any permit requirements established pursuant to 40 CFR 52.21 or under regulations approved pursuant to 40 CFR part 51, subpart I. Additionally, reductions are legally and practicably enforceable if the reductions can be independently verified; violations of the program that generated the credits are defined and those liable for the violations can be identified; access to the emissions-related information underlying the credits is available; and the public can file civil lawsuits to enforce violations.[29] The EPA's approval of Rule 205 into the SIP ensures that MERCs issued under the rule are federally enforceable. In addition, after determining that the requested reductions meet the certification criteria, the permits that MCAQD issues pursuant to its SIP-approved NNSR program incorporate requirements that make the reductions in qualifying emissions federally enforceable.[30 31]
Based on our evaluation, we find that Rule 205 ensures that offsetting emissions reductions will be permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable consistent with the requirements of CAA section 173 and 40 CFR 51.165.
Comment 2: The commenter stated that Rule 205 measures emissions reductions solely at the tailpipe, relies on the EPA's MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) based emission factors, and excludes “upstream NOX and VOC emissions associated with electricity generation and transmission needed to power replacement battery electric vehicles.” Therefore, the commenter believes these actions can, in effect, overstate actual emissions reductions. Because CAA section 173(c)(1) requires emissions increases to be offset by the “actual emissions” of such air pollutant within the nonattainment area, the commenter requested the EPA account for upstream ( printed page 69698) “lifecycle” emissions increases associated with charging electric vehicles by “requiring MCAQD to include, at minimum, a qualitative disclosure in each MERC application identifying the electricity source and associated upstream NOX and VOC emissions.”
Response 2: The EPA disagrees with the claim that to approve Rule 205 the EPA must account for upstream “lifecycle” emissions potentially associated with charging electric vehicles by requiring the MCAQD to include a qualitative disclosure in each MERC application identifying the electricity source and upstream NOX and VOC emissions. As an initial matter, we note that Rule 205 is designed to be broadly applicable, and MERCs can be generated using any fuel type ( e.g., replacing a diesel engine with a lower-emitting diesel engine). That is, Rule 205 is fuel neutral and not every MERC application will be for electric vehicles, as suggested by the comment.
The commenter's concern that the use of MOVES can overstate the actual emissions reductions eligible for offsets when a vehicle is replaced with an electric vehicle raises a hypothetical, fact-specific issue that is best evaluated in the context of an individual MERC application. The commenter specifically cited to the requirement in CAA section 173(c)(1) that requires emissions increases to “be offset by an equal or greater reduction, as applicable, in the actual emissions of such air pollutant from the same or other sources in the area.” As we explained in our proposal, this means the emissions reductions must be “real” and not a theoretical reduction in the source's potential to emit; in other words, it requires that each offset represents emissions that have been taken out of the air.[32] The requirements of Rule 205 ensure that this requirement will be met. For example, before granting MERCs, Rule 205 requires the MCAQD to evaluate whether the emissions reductions will be real and include an opportunity for public comment on the Department's evaluation.[33] The rule also defines “real” as “[a] reduction in actual emissions previously released into the air resulting from a physical change or change to the method of operation by a generator.” [34] Thus, no revisions to Rule 205 are needed to ensure CAA section 173(c)(1) will be met. While the MERC calculation methodology in Appendix A of Rule 205 is meant to be applicable to most situations, if the MCAQD determines that not all of the emissions reductions for a specific project would be real, then the MERC generator could potentially obtain approval from the MCAQD and the EPA for an alternative MERC calculation method.[35] Regardless of the calculation method used, the Department must determine that the requested MERCs will result in real, quantifiable, federally enforceable, permanent, and surplus emissions reductions prior to the MERC generator requesting a permit or permit revision to impose conditions to make the emissions reductions permanent and enforceable.[36]
Comment 3: The commenter stated that Appendix A of Rule 205, which contains the equation used to quantify the number of MERCs, and the MCAQD's EIP support document effectively only addresses electric vehicles. The MOVES model does not “separately represent hybrid, plug-in hybrid, CNG [compressed natural gas], LNG [liquefied natural gas], or other alternative-fuel vehicles as distinct source types” and, as a result, non-electric vehicle projects may rely on default MOVES assumptions that do not reflect actual emissions and undermine the “quantifiability and integrity of generated MERCs.”
Response 3: The EPA disagrees with the commenter's claim that the quantification method in Rule 205 can only be used to generate MERCs through replacing vehicles with electric vehicles. In 2025, MCAQD revised the quantification method in Rule 205 to ensure the rule is fuel neutral. Owners/operators of vehicle fleets can opt to choose any available vehicle type as a replacement as long as it would emit less NOX and VOC, including diesel, compressed natural gas, gasoline/diesel hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and electric vehicles.
The emission rates within MOVES differ by the vehicle type and by the fuel type used, as well as other aspects of vehicles and their activity.[37 38] Rule 205 identifies fuel type as one of the data points required to run MOVES.[39] Therefore, the necessary inputs to quantify MERCs are well defined in Rule 205, ensuring emissions from all fuel types are quantifiable under Rule 205.[40 41]
Comment 4: The commenter stated that the surplus requirement mandates that credited reductions must not otherwise be required by the CAA and, therefore, MERCs must account for tightening Federal vehicle standards. The commenter stated that as EPA emissions standards progressively reduce NOX and non-methane organic gas emissions, “the emissions factors embedded in MOVES will increasingly reflect reductions mandated by [F]ederal law,” which would not qualify as voluntary or surplus reductions. Essentially, “[r]ule 205 addresses surplus only at the point of application and fails to ensure that credits remain `surplus' as [F]ederal vehicle standards tighten.”
Response 4: We disagree with the commenter's claim that Rule 205 fails to ensure that MERCs remain surplus as Federal vehicle standards tighten. While not specifically stated in the comment, we assume the commenter is referring to the concept of “fleet turnover,” where the totality of the vehicles in an area will emit less air pollutants over time because of the natural cycle of vehicle owners replacing their vehicles with newer models, which are typically subject to more stringent vehicle emissions standards. Because CAA section 173(c)(2) expressly states that “[e]mission reductions otherwise required by [the CAA] shall not be creditable as emissions reductions for purposes of any such offset requirement,” emissions reductions used to demonstrate attainment of the NAAQS or to meet transportation conformity requirements would not be creditable for NNSR offset purposes under CAA section 173.
To ensure MERCs are surplus and meet the requirements of CAA section 173(c)(2), the MCAQD Rule 205 ( printed page 69699) submittal explains that the Maricopa Association of Governments (MAG) [42] will address this by adding 1,000 tpy of NOX and 500 tpy of VOC emissions into the emissions inventory for its new ozone “Moderate” area plan for the 2015 ozone NAAQS.[43] This line item represents the maximum number of MERCs and/or nonroad engine emission reduction credits (NERCs) that will be creditable through Rule 205 and MCAQD Rule 204, “Emission Offsets Generated by Voluntary Nonroad Engine Emission Reductions,” revised on November 5, 2025 (“Rule 204”).[44] Effectively, this ensures MERCs and NERCs generated through Rules 205 and 204, respectively, will be excluded from SIP modeling and cannot be accounted for in the State's attainment demonstration for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. Regarding transportation conformity, the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal explains that before the start of modeling for a transportation plan or transportation improvement program conformity, the MCAQD will notify MAG of each individual MERC project so that the reductions from each project are not included in the corresponding transportation conformity analysis, consistent with the interagency consultation process required by 40 CFR 93.112.[45]
These actions by the MCAQD and MAG related to attainment plans and transportation conformity ensure that Rule 205 will only allow surplus emissions reductions to be creditable for NNSR offset purposes and that Arizona will not “double-count” emissions reductions when developing SIP attainment demonstrations.
Comment 5.a: The commenter asserted that Rule 205 is deficient because it does not specify whether ongoing monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements applicable to MERC generators must be preserved when the generator's business changes hands, restructures, expands, or shuts down. The commenter asserted that this omission is a legal defect.
Response 5.a: We disagree that Rule 205 is deficient because it does not specifically state what happens to ongoing requirements in Rule 205 when the MERC generator's business changes hands, restructures, expands, or shuts down. Under Rule 205, MERC generators will be issued permits that contain the applicable monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements.[46] If the owner/operator named on the permit were to change as a result of a business changing hands, restructuring, expanding, or shutting down, the MCAQD's SIP-approved New Source Review (NSR) program provides a process for ensuring that permit requirements remain in effect, and this process would apply to MERC generators.[47] MCAQD Rule 200, “Permit Requirements,” revised on December 11, 2019 (“Rule 200”), describes the requirements for transferring a permit, including, but not limited to, a signed statement and acceptance of responsibility for the permit by the new permit holder.[48] To the extent the commenter is concerned about the integrity of MERCs as a result of a business changing hands, restructuring, expanding, or shutting down, Rule 205 contains provisions for ensuring the ongoing integrity of MERCs and includes requirements to address potential shortfalls in emissions reductions.[49]
Comment 5.b: The commenter stated that the requirement for MERC generators in Rule 205 to track, for 20 years, that a new or retrofitted vehicle is only replaced with a vehicle that is certified to the same or lower emission standards is a “de facto constraint on future fleet decisions.” As an example, the commenter stated that a company that switches to electric vehicles but leases vehicles on a three-year cycle could be prohibited from reverting to internal combustion engines at the end of the lease term, which the commenter asserted would effectively function as a long-term electric vehicle mandate. The commenter concluded that the rule therefore “raises significant preemption concerns absent a [CAA] [s]ection 209 waiver.”
Response 5.b: We disagree that Rule 205 functions as a long-term electric vehicle mandate that raises preemption concerns under CAA section 209. CAA section 209(a) prohibits States from setting or enforcing new motor vehicle emissions standards unless a waiver is granted by the EPA under CAA section 209(b).[50] Here, there is no State action to set or enforce a new motor vehicle emissions standard. Rule 205 is merely an administrative rule to facilitate the creation and trading of MERCs for use as offsets by stationary sources. Participation in the MERC generating program is voluntary. If a fleet owner or operator voluntarily chooses to generate MERCs by replacing a vehicle with an electric vehicle, then Rule 205 requires the MERC generator to maintain the same level of emissions reductions for 20 years to meet the offset integrity criteria. As stated previously, Rule 205 is fuel neutral and does not restrict the type of vehicle replacement that qualifies for generating MERCs. If a MERC generator finds that replacing a vehicle with an electric vehicle would be too restrictive on future vehicle fleet decisions, then the MERC generator can choose a replacement vehicle type with emission rates the MERC generator can more confidently maintain.
No comments were submitted that changed our assessment of the approvability of the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal as described in our proposed action. Therefore, as authorized in CAA section 110(k)(3), the EPA is approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal by adding MCAQD Rule 205 into the federally enforceable portion of the Arizona SIP and adding the MCAQD's EIP support document into the non-regulatory portion of the Arizona SIP.
V. Incorporation by Reference
In this document, the EPA is finalizing regulatory text that includes incorporation by reference. In accordance with requirements of 1 CFR 51.5, the EPA is finalizing the incorporation by reference of MCAQD ( printed page 69700) Rule 205, “Emission Offsets Generated by Voluntary Mobile Source Emission Reductions,” revised on May 21, 2025, which establishes a federally enforceable program allowing fleet vehicle owners/operators to generate ERCs through voluntary on-road mobile source emissions reductions under the CAA. Therefore, these materials have been approved by the EPA for inclusion in the SIP, have been incorporated by reference by the EPA into that plan, are fully federally enforceable under CAA sections 110 and 113 as of the effective date of the final rulemaking of the EPA's approval, and will be incorporated by reference in the next update to the SIP compilation.[51] The EPA has made, and will continue to make, these documents available through https://www.regulations.gov and at the EPA Region IX Office (please contact the person identified in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section of this preamble for more information).
VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
Under the CAA, the Administrator is required to approve a SIP submission that complies with the provisions of the CAA and applicable Federal regulations (42 U.S.C. 7410(k); 40 CFR 52.02(a)). Thus, in reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA's role is to approve State choices, provided that they meet the criteria of the CAA. Accordingly, this action merely approves State law as meeting Federal requirements and does not impose additional requirements beyond those imposed by State law. For that reason, this action:
Is not a significant regulatory action subject to review by the Office of Management and Budget underExecutive Order 12866 (58 FR 51735, October 4, 1993);
Is not anExecutive Order 14192 (90 FR 9065, February 6, 2025) regulatory action because this action is not significant under Executive Order 12866;
Does not impose an information collection burden under the provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq.);
Is certified as not having a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.);
Does not contain any unfunded mandate or significantly or uniquely affect small governments, as described in the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (Pub. L. 104-4);
Does not have federalism implications as specified inExecutive Order 13132 (64 FR 43255, August 10, 1999);
Is not subject toExecutive Order 13045 (62 FR 19885, April 23, 1997) because it approves a State program;
Is not a significant regulatory action subject toExecutive Order 13211 (66 FR 28355, May 22, 2001); and
Is not subject to requirements of section 12(d) of the National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (15 U.S.C. 272 note) because application of those requirements would be inconsistent with the CAA.
In addition, the SIP is not approved to apply on any Indian reservation land or in any other area where the EPA or an Indian Tribe has demonstrated that a Tribe has jurisdiction. In those areas of Indian country, the rule does not have Tribal implications and will not impose substantial direct costs on Tribal governments or preempt Tribal law as specified by Executive Order 13175 (65 FR 67249, November 9, 2000).
This action is subject to the Congressional Review Act, and the EPA will submit a rule report to each House of the Congress and to the Comptroller General of the United States. This action is not a “major rule” as defined by 5 U.S.C. 804(2).
Under section 307(b)(1) of the Clean Air Act, petitions for judicial review of this action must be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the appropriate circuit by January 4, 2027. Filing a petition for reconsideration by the Administrator of this final rule does not affect the finality of this action for the purposes of judicial review nor does it extend the time within which a petition for judicial review may be filed, and shall not postpone the effectiveness of such rule or action. This action may not be challenged later in proceedings to enforce its requirements ( See CAA section 307(b)(2)).

title: How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan
zh_title: 如何防止台湾能源检疫
summary: 如何防止台湾能源检疫 - 大西洋理事会北京正在为台湾能源检疫奠定基础。经济、政治、技术和军事因素可能导致能源检疫风险在 2028 年和 2029 年达到顶峰。为了阻止这种强制行动，美国及其盟国应与台湾合作，通过支持上述所有能源战略来加强其安全，重点是向台湾北部供应用于发电的柴油。中共总书记习近平多次明确表态：
content:
如何防止台湾能源检疫 - 大西洋理事会
北京正在为台湾的能源检疫奠定基础。
经济、政治、技术和军事因素可能导致能源检疫风险在 2028 年和 2029 年达到峰值。
为了阻止这种胁迫行动，美国及其盟国应与台湾合作，通过支持上述所有能源战略来加强台湾的安全，重点是向台湾北部供应用于发电的柴油。
中国共产党总书记习近平一贯明确表示台湾应该与中国大陆“统一”，并在2013年表示“两岸长期存在的政治分歧……总不能一代一代传下去”。习近平还在 2026 年 5 月与美国总统唐纳德·特朗普会面时警告称，在台湾问题上可能会发生“冲突甚至冲突”。这件事似乎不是决心的问题，而是时机的问题。出于政治、经济和技术原因，习近平可能对台湾采取行动的风险可能在 2028 年和 2029 年达到顶峰。
为了实现其长期的统一目标，北京可能会尝试通过非动能措施胁迫台湾。隔离的模糊性和灵活性可能使其成为对习近平特别有吸引力的选择。北京可以宣称，检疫——允许一些船只通过，同时拒绝其他船只，特别是油轮和液化天然气（LNG）运输船——是一种国内执法措施，而不是一种战争行为。有证据表明，习近平的军队已经在为隔离而不是入侵进行演练，因为中国海警在台湾以东海域持续存在，并试图将封锁商业交通正常化，从而挑战台北的海上控制。
切断台湾能源供应的隔离作为一种强制工具尤其有效。台湾几乎没有本土生产石油、天然气或煤炭，这使得它几乎完全依赖海运进口碳氢化合物。北京很早就明白能源安全在台湾突发事件中的重要性。目前，它不太容易受到能源中断的影响，并准备好承受根据需要切断部分能源进口的情况。
对台湾实施能源隔离对美国来说将是一件严重的事情。台湾因其地理位置、深厚的技术专长以及作为人工智能（AI）供应链关键节点的地位而对华盛顿具有重要的战略意义。中国吞并台湾将使全球经济和战略力量平衡向有利于北京的方向倾斜，美国决策者必须避免对台湾采取强制行动，否则可能升级为军事冲突。碰撞的危险怎么强调都不为过：美国和中国都是拥有强大常规军队的核武器国家；技术超级大国，尤其是人工智能领域；以及拥有一系列强制工具的庞大经济体。
应对这些风险需要大量军事投资，但联盟决策者不应忽视近期能源隔离的严重风险。为了阻止台湾的能源隔离，美国和其他民主国家应与台湾合作，通过上述所有方法以及快速部署燃料来源（特别是柴油）的战略优先事项来加强其能源安全。美国，T

How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan - Atlantic Council
Beijing is laying the groundwork for an energy quarantine of Taiwan.
Economic, political, technical, and military factors could lead energy quarantine risks to peak in 2028 and 2029.
To deter this coercive action, the United States and allies should work with Taiwan to bolster its security through support for an all-of-the-above energy strategy, concentrating on supplying northern Taiwan with diesel for power generation.
Chinese Communist Party (CCP) General Secretary Xi Jinping has consistently made clear his view that Taiwan should be “reunified” with mainland China, stating in 2013 that “long-standing cross-Strait political differences … cannot be passed down from generation to generation (总不能一代一代传下去).” Xi also warned of “clashes or even conflicts” over Taiwan in his May 2026 meeting with US President Donald Trump. The matter appears to be a question not of determination but of timing. For political, economic, and technical reasons, the risk that Xi might move against Taiwan could peak in 2028 and 2029.
To achieve its longstanding unification goal, Beijing might attempt to coerce Taiwan via non-kinetic measures. The ambiguity and flexibility of a quarantine could render it an especially attractive option for Xi. Beijing could claim that a quarantine—allowing some ships to pass while turning back others, especially oil tankers and liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers—is a domestic law-enforcement measure rather than an act of war. There is some evidence that Xi’s forces are already rehearsing for a quarantine rather than an invasion, as the Chinese coast guard is maintaining a continuous presence in waters east of Taiwan and trying to normalize interdictions of live commercial traffic, thereby challenging Taipei’s maritime control.
A quarantine to cut off Taiwan’s energy supply would be particularly effective as a coercive tool. Taiwan has virtually no indigenous production of oil, natural gas, or coal, rendering it almost totally reliant on seaborne imports for hydrocarbons. Beijing has long understood the importance of energy security in a Taiwan contingency. It is currently much less vulnerable to an energy outage and is prepared to weather a cutoff of some of its own energy imports as needed.
An energy quarantine of Taiwan would be a grave matter for the United States. Taiwan is strategically important to Washington due to its geography, deep technological expertise, and position as a critical node in artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains. China’s absorption of Taiwan would tilt the global economic and strategic balance of power in Beijing’s favor, making it imperative for US policymakers to avert coercive action against the island, which could escalate into a military conflict. It is difficult to overstate the dangers of a collision: the United States and China are nuclear-armed nations with powerful conventional militaries; technological superpowers, especially in AI; and huge economies with an array of coercive tools.
Countering these risks will require substantial military investments, but coalition policymakers should not overlook the serious risks of a near-term energy quarantine. To deter an energy quarantine of Taiwan, the United States and other democracies should work with Taiwan to reinforce its energy security with an all-of-the-above approach and the strategic prioritization of rapidly deployable fuel sources, especially diesel. The United States, Taiwan, and other actors should immediately begin preparing for a contingency by deploying a diesel-generation supply chain across Taiwan, especially in the energy-scarce northern regions surrounding the capital, Taipei. That will include diesel production at refineries, distributed storage, and ultimately generators for power supply. The humble diesel generator could be a key determinant in the future of global power.
The groundwork: Beijing is mitigating its own energy vulnerabilities
In 2003, then General Secretary Hu Jintao warned that China faced the “Malacca Dilemma,” or “马六甲困局.” Hu noted that Beijing’s reliance on seaborne oil imports from the Middle East navigating the Malacca Strait near Singapore raised acute vulnerabilities, as shipments could be interdicted by the US Navy. More than two decades later, Beijing is becoming increasingly self-sufficient in energy overall and in transportation fuels such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. While Beijing will not achieve true independence in transportation fuels for several years, it is on its way to effectively mitigating the Malacca Dilemma.
Beijing has been seeking to mitigate this dilemma via a combination of reduced transport fuel demand (largely from vehicle electrification), elevated domestic crude oil production, overland crude oil pipeline imports (largely from Russia), maximizing refinery production of transportation fuels, and tapping unprecedentedly large petroleum stockpiles. Beijing’s growing oil security will enable it to increasingly decouple from international markets and allow it to act more aggressively vis-à-vis Taiwan.
Electrification has been fundamental to China’s energy self-sufficiency drive. Electricity’s share of final energy in China has grown from about 5 percent in 1990 to nearly 30 percent today, an increase of about 1 percentage point every year, and will soon surpass the percentage share of every Group of Seven (G7) economy. Mainland China’s power generation capacity has risen from 138 gigawatts in 1990 to over 4,000 gigawatts by May 2026; China has also added 24.2 million charging points (not stations) and, by 2023, had already provided $230 billion in government support to its EV industry. Finally, many Chinese cities have mandated that ride share vehicles and urban logistics vehicles must be “new energy vehicles”—in practice, usually battery EVs. These measures have enabled China to become the undeniable world leader in vehicle electrification.
Vehicle electrification rapidly mitigates Beijing’s exposure to the Malacca Dilemma by directly reducing gasoline and diesel demand, especially in politically-sensitive first tier cities. According to the International Energy Agency, electric vehicles are set to reduce Chinese oil demand by about a total of 2.7 million barrels per day (MMbpd) by 2030. In a July 2025 analysis, Rhodium Group found that China’s total electric vehicle fleet already displaced more than 1 MMbpd, with battery electric vehicles beginning to make significant headway in trucking fleets that rely primarily on diesel.
For these reasons, the International Energy Agency and others hold that Chinese gasoline and diesel demand has likely already peaked. Deployment of advanced, energy-dense batteries to medium and heavy-duty vehicles would further reduce diesel consumption, alleviating Beijing’s chief transport fuel constraint in a crisis. Adoption of advanced batteries in heavy-duty vehicles might rise sharply over the next year or two.
As it reduces its transport fuel demand via vehicle electrification, China has also stockpiled about 1.2 billion barrels of crude oil in December 2025 in total petroleum reserves, by far the world’s largest. While Beijing is drawing down oil inventories amid the oil market disruptions from the US–Iran war, storage levels remain elevated and can be expanded if the conflict winds down.
In the case of a quarantine, Beijing would rely heavily on supply flows of oil, not only on stock withdrawals.
Here it’s useful to divide Beijing’s oil supplies into different resilience tiers. Tier 1, the most secure tier, is China’s own domestic crude oil production, which ticked up from 3.8 million barrels per day (MMbpd) in 2017 to about 4.4 MMbpd in the first seven months of 2026, covering about 30 percent of domestic demand before the US–Iran war.
In addition to its own domestic production, China can also obtain additional volumes from relatively secure overland pipelines in Tier 2A. China’s secure overland crude oil shipments total about 0.8 MMbpd. This is split between the Russia-to-China leg of the East Siberia–Pacific Ocean pipeline, with deliveries of about 600,000 barrels per day (b/d), and the Atasu–Alashankou pipeline, which brings both Russian and Kazakhstani oil via Kazakhstan and delivers roughly 200,000 b/d to Xinjiang. Existing Russian and Kazakhstani overland pipelines have delivery capacity of about 1.2 MMbpd; in a crisis, China would likely be able to access these full volumes, albeit at a possible premium.
Tier 2B consists of Russian maritime crude imports. Russia typically ships about 0.75 MMbpd to China from its Kozmino port, near Vladivostok, with other export terminals typically providing about 0.25 MMbpd. The US Navy and coalitional navies would weigh carefully whether to interdict Russian ships and disable Russian exports. Targeting Russian vessels and infrastructure risks horizontal and perhaps even vertical escalation, but in a Taiwan contingency the benefits of disabling Russian energy shipments to the Chinese mainland could, under some conditions, outweigh that risk. To mitigate the risks of maritime transit, Beijing and Moscow might expand the capacity of the mainland China leg of the East Siberia–Pacific Ocean pipeline, “promoting” perhaps 0.8 MMbpd from Tier 2B into Tier 2A.
Tier 3 is the 200,000 b/d pipeline from Myanmar, which delivers oil to Yunnan. This source can be thought of as only quasi-overland, however, as it relies on maritime imports to the Made Island oil import terminal that could be interdicted relatively easily.
Tier 4 imports, meanwhile, consist of all other maritime sources.
China can reliably access about 5.6 MMbpd of crude oil supply from domestic and overland sources if all existing pipeline capacity is utilized. Adding about another 1 MMbpd from Russian maritime imports would bring the total to nearly 6.6 MMbpd. If its most secure supplies are operable in a crisis, then about 30 percent of China’s supplies would hinge on Russia, demonstrating Beijing’s interest in maintaining close ties with Moscow.
Turning to demand, China’s refinery runs for crude oil stood at about 15.2 MMbpd in January–February 2026 (assuming 7.33 barrels/ton). Amid the US–Iran war, these runs fell to about 12.5 MMbpd in June, per China’s National Bureau of Statistics. In a contingency, Beijing could again sharply reduce its demand, including in petrochemicals, which accounts for about 25 percent of Chinese oil demand and largely serves the export market. In addition, Beijing could order refineries to maximize output of transportation fuels, including diesel and jet fuel for its military.
Given that total domestic supply from production and secure import capacity equals 6.6 MMbpd, and assuming total refinery runs of 12.5 MMbpd seen in June 2026, China would face a daily deficit of about 5.9 MMbpd in a contingency today. Assuming that China has reserves of about 1.1 billion barrels of crude oil after Iran war-related drawdowns, and that it would be able to draw inventories to only 20 percent before facing constraints from geographic dispersion and tank draw, China would be able to sustain at least one hundred and fifty days of civilian and military activities before reaching physical shortage.
By 2030, however, Beijing will very likely enjoy far greater oil security. Tier 1 and 2A overland crude supplies could very easily rise to 6.8 MMbpd on higher domestic production and greater overland tie-ins with Russian and Central Asian crude oil pipelines. Crude oil demand, meanwhile, could fall to 11.5 MMbpd amid vehicle electrification, leaving a deficit of 4.7 MMbpd. Assuming 1.2 billion barrels of crude oil reserves and a maximum drawdown of inventories to 20 percent, Beijing could likely cover at least two hundred days of refinery runs in a contingency by 2030. Beijing may soon be able to withstand an oil blockade for well over half a year, and perhaps much longer if it continues to increase the size of its oil reserves, can still access Russian maritime imports, or accelerates vehicle electrification.
The United States’ implicit answer to a potential Taiwan quarantine has been to impose a counter-blockade of China’s oil imports. That strategy is increasingly outdated. Policymakers in Washington, Taipei, Tokyo, and beyond need to understand this dangerous new reality, insulate against an energy quarantine, and find other sources of coercive leverage against Beijing.
Taiwan’s exposure: Two likely scenarios for an energy quarantine
Taiwan’s indigenous energy production (including nuclear energy generation) as a percentage of all energy demand declined from 8.3 percent to 5.3 percent from 2016 to 2025.
Taiwan’s reserves of oil, coal, and LNG are required to cover ninety days, thirty days, and eleven days of consumption for each commodity, respectively, although inventories typically cover more. In March 2026, the Ministry of Economic Affairs reported oil, coal, and LNG on-hand inventories of one hundred and fifty days, forty days, and eleven days, respectively. Still, Taiwan’s actual days of consumption covered vary based on several factors, including seasonal weather patterns, its ability to export goods such as semiconductors from its energy-intensive industrial sector, and the continued operation of refineries.
Other regional democracies’ roles in a Taiwan contingency could be constrained by their energy-related vulnerabilities. Japan and South Korea also have limited storage inventories, while other US allies such as the Philippines and Australia are themselves highly reliant on energy imports. Australia’s fuel dependency is staggering: it relies on imports for 83 percent of all refined petroleum products. The coalition has serious work to do to improve its collective energy resilience, and to do so quickly.
If Beijing attempted to subjugate Taiwan via an energy quarantine, two scenarios are most likely. Beijing might straightforwardly implement a quarantine or even blockade of Taiwan, attempting to interdict any inbound energy shipments via its coast guard by claiming a legal pretext.
Alternatively, Beijing might try an indirect approach by exploiting or even stimulating a future Middle Eastern oil crisis. Surging oil prices would disproportionately damage Beijing’s regional rivals, which are relatively reliant on oil imports even as China increasingly turns into a self-sufficient electrotech state.
Timing the risk: Quarantine dangers might peak in 2028 and 2029
The dangers of an energy-weighted geopolitical crisis over Taiwan are already serious but might peak in 2028 and 2029 due to economics, politics, Taiwan’s electricity reserve margins, military readiness, and AI. Mainland China’s economy is showing significant strain even as Taiwan’s powers ahead; both Taiwan and the United States will hold key elections in 2028; Taiwan’s electricity reserve margin is on track to reach dangerously low levels in this period; US military readiness levels might be damaged by protracted deployments in other theaters; and while AI timelines are highly unpredictable, the United States might begin to experience takeoff growth, which could enable it to establish permanent technological dominance. Given these factors, and his own age, Xi might believe by 2028 that he has a limited window of opportunity to act.
Beijing has economic reasons for attempting to control Taiwan sooner rather than later. If economic trends continue, Beijing’s comparative performance legitimacy will weaken vis-à-vis Taiwan through January 2028. Taiwan’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth is projected to reach an astonishing 11 percent in 2026. While most economic growth is concentrated in the tech sector, real median incomes are rising, Taiwan’s government is flush enough to disburse cash payments, the fiscal budget is balanced, and Taiwan’s debt-to-GDP ratio is the lowest in East Asia. Taiwan’s economy is doing well, even if growth will likely decelerate.
Conversely, while Beijing retains formidable economic power, mainland China’seconomy shows significant weakness. Growth rates are undeniably slowing. Chinese debt levels are in a “league of their own,” according to Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. Logan Wright, partner at Rhodium Group, warns that Beijing’s growth model is “fundamentally broken” and faces “steady decay.” The risks to mainland China’s economy may provide added urgency for Xi to pursue an energy quarantine of Taiwan and coerce it into accepting Beijing’s rule. Assuming current economic trends continue, Taiwan’s living standards will further outpace mainland China’s, significantly damaging the appeal of unification for Taiwan’s voters.
Taiwan will hold its next presidential election in January 2028. While nothing is certain, the outcome of the election is likely to lead to intense discomfort in Beijing (as the author has been warning since June 2026). In most democracies, rising living standards benefit the incumbent party. That means that the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) is likely to prevail in 2028 presidential elections, assuming Taiwan maintains robust economic growth, which is likely; the DPP is also favored to obtain a majority in the Legislative Yuan, Taiwan’s parliament. Living standards are not the only variable affecting elections, and the composition of candidates from the three main parties in Taiwan will matter greatly for the 2028 election, governing, and cross-Strait relations. Nonetheless, initial indications suggest that political economy trends in Taiwan do not appear to be moving in Beijing’s favor.
As political economy theory might predict, Taiwan’s voters may be rewarding the incumbent party for producing rising living standards. In a stunning reversal from even a few months ago, the DPP is now favored to win the Taipei mayoral race. The approval rating of President Lai Ching-te of the DPP has steadily climbed for months and is at its highest level since April 2025. Other parties could still win in 2028, especially if economic growth falters, perhaps due to an AI market correction in the United States. Nonetheless, assuming robust (and reasonably well-distributed) economic growth continues, then the DPP will likely win both the presidential and the Legislative Yuan elections in January 2028, to Beijing’s immense dissatisfaction.
The United States will also hold its own presidential election in November 2028. Political trends indicate the election will be divisive, potentially distracting Americans from cross-Strait affairs. In addition, while Beijing eyes Trump warily, CCP leaders believe Trump’s transactional approach to governing might offer opportunities vis-à-vis Taiwan in the remainder of his term.
Technical factors will amplify political and economic risks. Taipower, Taiwan’s state-run power company, projects that its nighttime reserve margin will fall to about 8 percent in 2028 and 2029, far below its targeted reserve margin of 15 percent. If current trends continue, Taiwan’s power sector could face interrupted power supplies at night even in peacetime, which would make it even more vulnerable to a potential energy quarantine.
Beijing will also be weighing US military readiness and weapons inventory levels. Where these will stand in 2028 is uncertain, especially if the US conflict in Iran escalates.
AI timelines are their own huge source of uncertainty for 2028–2029. Beijing’s perception that the United States might be on the verge of establishing permanent technological dominance via powerful AI might upend Xi’s assumptions about the desirability of strategic patience and further incentivize Xi to intervene against Taiwan, the world’s most advanced chipmaker.
Finally, there is the human element: Xi’s own sense of destiny. If Taiwan shows no medium-term interest in peacefully or semi-peacefully uniting with the mainland, then Xi might feel pressure to act. He will turn seventy-five in 2028, will have limited patience for sentiment to change through future Taiwanese elections in 2032 or even 2036, and has made clear he does not want the Taiwan issue ‘passed down from generation to generation.’
All these considerations do not guarantee that 2028–2029 will be the peak period of risks in US-China relations. Risks might persist for decades. Still, these factors suggest a convergence of serious, compounding risks that warrant preparation and mitigation.
A strategy for deterrence: Taiwan and its friends should prepare for an energy contingency
There is a need to hedge against the foreseeable and highly consequential risk of an energy quarantine of Taiwan by Beijing, perhaps as early as 2028. While Taiwan is already taking important steps to enhance its energy resilience, its government and the United States must do more to prepare for this risk—and quickly.
To address its urgent energy security challenges, Taiwan needs to take an all-of-the-above approach to electricity generation while bolstering transmission.
Nuclear energy, in particular, is one of the most important pillars of Taiwan’s energy resiliency and should be expanded. Nuclear energy can operate continuously for at least eighteen months once fueled. Additionally, reactors are unlikely to be deliberately destroyed by CCP forces in a contingency. Beijing does not want to risk radiation exposure on the island it seeks to seize. Working with the United States, Japan, and other actors, Taiwan should seek to expand nuclear energy capacity as quickly as possible and start bringing its third nuclear power plant in Maanshan back online in 2028.
In addition to nuclear energy, Taiwan should expand use of LNG, renewables, oil for generation and transportation, and even coal where appropriate. Taiwan should continue to deepen ties with the US LNG complex; expanding natural gas storage capacity will also prove useful.
Finally, and most importantly, the island should adopt a “north diesel, south renewables” approach to electricity generation in preparation for a contingency, and resource this plan effectively.
Northern Taiwan, home to the capital Taipei, is critical. While northern Taiwan has some limited generation capacity, it is a net “importer” from the southern and central parts of the island, in what officials call ”南電北送,”or “send southern power north.” In a contingency, northern Taiwan might not be able to access power generation from the southern and central regions due to sabotage of power stations, substations, transmission lines, or other infrastructure. Moreover, northern Taiwan cannot rely on local renewables generation: Taipei’s solar capacity factor is, inadequately, about the same as Seattle’s, onshore land availability to build more solar is minimal, and regional offshore wind projects, while useful, generate less power in peak summer electricity demand months and also face sabotage risks. Finally, gas-fired power plants at Datan and Tunghsiao constitute the bulk of northern Taiwan’s indigenous power generation, and northern Taiwan’s LNG inventories are finite. If south-to-north transmission lines are cut in a contingency, Taipei could run out of electricity in under one month.
Fuels, especially diesel, are therefore critical for countering an energy quarantine or blockade of Taiwan, particularly one that could occur on a short timeline before the island has time to strengthen resilience through nuclear energy expansion and other tactics. Diesel can be stored for long periods of time and can provide distributed power without transmission wires, as Ukraine is proving. Additionally, diesel units can be deployed in a matter of weeks, although deploying this systematically will require more time and resources.
For approximately $10 billion in up-front capital expenditure plus an estimated $500 million a year to maintain, test, and rotate fuel, northern Taiwan could field about 2 gigawatts of diesel generation (based on author calculations). About half of the capital expenditures would be for a dedicated diesel fuel stockpile and dispersed, hardened storage; generators would account for the rest of the initial outlay. That level of diesel generation would provide enough power to keep hospitals, cooling stations, sanitation, telecom, and emergency services running in northern Taiwan for roughly five months without any power from the south. Taiwan could very likely stand up a first tranche of this system by summer 2027, when it could conduct power generation exercises as part of the Urban Resilience drills. The full buildout could be completed across 2028 and 2029 (and accelerated as needed).
In addition, Taiwan’s southern and central regions have large existing thermal generation power plants along with good-to-excellent renewable resources that cannot be interdicted easily, as they are less reliant on vulnerable, long-distance transmission lines and infrastructure that carry power north. In addition to strengthening the resilience of thermal power plants, including by stockpiling coal and natural gas reserves, Taiwan should increase construction of onshore solar and wind resources in the southern and central regions. Distributed renewables generation is much more difficult to take offline by Chinese forces in a quarantine, blockade, siege, or invasion.
With diesel generation in the north, generation from coal, gas, and nuclear power plants in the south, distributed renewables throughout the island, and aggressive rationing, Taiwan could extend its ability to endure an energy blockade from mere weeks to months.
Taiwan need not act alone, however. The United States has a critical role to play in averting a Taiwan energy contingency. US firms should engage with counterparts in Taiwan across all parts of the energy supply chain, including diesel generators and storage, LNG infrastructure, nuclear energy know-how, and solar and energy storage systems. The chief US contribution to Taiwan’s energy infrastructure might be preventing sabotage. In a contingency, CCP intelligence services would likely seek to degrade or disable Taiwan’s south-to-north power transmission lines and other energy infrastructure with either cyber or kinetic means. To accomplish kinetic sabotage, CCP intelligence services would use the full spectrum of their assets, including their connections with criminal networks. Accordingly, the United States should rotate a far greater number of energy, counternarcotics, and countersabotage personnel through Taiwan, drawing on the Department of Energy, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and other civilian security agencies, through the American Institute in Taiwan.
China’s vulnerabilities: Leverage that could enforce stability
In addition to precautionary defensive measures, Washington, Taipei, and other actors should find other forms of leverage over Beijing. China’s food vulnerabilities are significant, while its steel industry relies extensively on Australian iron ore imports. Analysts should carefully scrutinize these commodities, especially if China begins to build inventories.
The most effective form of leverage vis-à-vis Beijing, however, could be economic and financial. China’s economic growth model might be broken. China remains highly reliant on other countries absorbing its overcapacity, as net exports’ contribution to GDP growth stood at 32.7 percent, the highest level since 1997. Far from successfully rebalancing, China’s economic and financial model has become more reliant on exports, investments, and debt, raising the likelihood of a painful correction. If Beijing attempted to coerce Taiwan, including through an energy quarantine, China’s ability to reach export markets might be imperiled due to a combination of economic, financial, cyber, and other measures. If China loses substantial access to export markets due to an unwise attempt to coerce Taipei, the risks for its economic, financial, social, and ultimately political stability could be profound.
While the risks of an energy quarantine are significant and rising, Taipei and Washington are well positioned to mitigate these dangers. Taiwan is already making great strides in enhancing its energy resilience. It should build on these efforts by building new generation for the long term and, especially, leveraging diesel as a near-term bridge solution. Similarly, Washington should take a more active role in opposing unilateral changes to the status quo by either side. Washington should underscore its continued commitment to the “One China” policy, anchored to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiqués, and the Six Assurances, while warning Beijing not to undertake aggression. If Taipei and Washington can see through this moment of danger, they could settle into a period of relative stability.
Joseph Webster is a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global Energy Center and the Indo-Pacific Security Initiative; he also edits the independent China-Russia Report. This analysis reflects his personal opinion.

content:
Fundraiser by Yiran Zhang : Help a girl to complete her university study
Yiran Zhang is organizing this fundraiser.
大家好，我是张怡然，是一名加州大学戴维斯分校社会学专业的大二学生。在我父亲的支持下，我来到美国留学。我父亲，鲁扬，是一位努力推动中国人权和民主的著名诗人和作家。
2020年5月，他在社交媒体平台上发表了一段视频，要求中国的执政党及其领导人下台，给中国人民民主权利。（https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a8Bb0FxZXZw) 因此，我父亲被逮捕，被判罪名"煽动颠覆国家政权"。审判初期，我母亲为父亲聘请的律师被政府拒绝接见，而政府另外指定的官派律师拒绝向我们透露父亲被关押和审判的具体情况。2022年7月26日，我母亲接到法院判决结果，被告知我爸爸被判刑6年。这令我们痛心万分。他的案件卷宗里根本没有任何实质性的足以判罪的证据。此外，法院以此案是“秘密案件”为由，拒绝给我妈妈案件的判决书。当前，我爸爸已经提出上诉。
我父亲被抓前，书法生意做得很好。但是他被抓后，书法生意被迫关闭，还使得我们家平白无故欠下很多债务。更糟糕的是，我母亲的所有银行账户也都被冻结，本来办的教学辅导班也被勒令停止。
我父亲接下来还要面对数年的牢狱囚禁，我家里还有年迈的老人需要赡养，经济负担使我母亲感到绝望，不堪重负。现在，由于我的学习费用很高，她无法负担我在加州大学戴维斯分校的学费。中国的公安部门以我出国留学为借口，限制我母亲的行动和言论自由。我和我母亲都知道，我的学习和前途是我们家唯一的希望，所以我不想从大学辍学。因此，我必须在这里筹集资金以维持我未来的学习。
请帮助我，一个勇敢而真诚的中国政治异见人士的孩子，完成我的大学学业。您的帮助将是对我、我的家庭和中国人权的重要支持!
Hello everyone, my name is Yiran Zhang, a sophomore majoring in sociology at the University of California, Davis. With the support of my father, I came to the United States to study abroad. My father, Lu Yang, was a famous poet and writer who strived to promote human rights and democracy in China.
In May 2020, he posted a video on social media platforms demanding that China's ruling party and its leaders step down and give the Chinese people democratic rights. (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a8Bb0FxZXZw) My father was arrested and charged with "inciting subversion of state power". At the beginning of the trial, the lawyer hired by my mother was denied access by the government, and another government-appointed lawyer refused to disclose to us the specific circumstances of my father's detention and trial. On July 26, 2022, my mother received the court verdict and was told that my father was sentenced to 6 years in prison. This saddens us greatly. There is simply no substantial incriminating evidence in his case file. In addition, the court refused to give my mother a paper copy of the verdict on the grounds that the case was a "secret case." Currently, my dad has filed an appeal.
Before my father was arrested, his calligraphy business was doing well. But after he was arrested, the calligraphy business was forced to close, and our family owed a lot of debt for no reason. Even worse, all of my mother's bank accounts were frozen, and the tutoring classes she held were demanded to stop.
The financial burden makes my mother feel hopeless and overwhelmed. Now, due to the high cost of my studies, she could hardly afford my tuition at UC Davis. At the same time, she also needs to provide for the elderly. China's public security authorities used my right to study abroad as an excuse to restrict my mother's freedom of movement and speech. My mother and I all know that my studies and future are the only hope for the family, so I don't want to drop out of college. Thus, I have to raise funds here to sustain my future studies.
Please help me, a brave and sincere child of a Chinese political dissident, to finish my university studies. Your help will be an important support for me, my family and human rights in China!

content:
如果黑客能夠控制超市的冷凍櫃，其他科技設備又有多脆弱？ - BBC News 中文
Author, 希奧娜·麥卡勒姆（Shiona McCallum）
歐洲多地超市近日遭遇一起疑似網絡攻擊，影響其冷藏櫃和冷凍櫃，並引發外界對互聯網連接硬件漏洞的憂慮。這些硬件涵蓋工業機械，以至日常家用電器。
連接互聯網的智能設備可以包括冰箱、中央供暖系統，甚至洗衣機。
雖然這類設備因此更容易被遠程控制，但理論上，任何接入網絡的設備都有可能被惡意行為者利用。
然而，這並不意味著黑客能輕易取得控制權，而且大型品牌通常會投入大量資源，確保其產品的安全性。
過去曾在部分設備中發現漏洞。2015年，研究人員展示了三星（Samsung）智能冰箱中的一項漏洞，如何讓他們攔截互聯網流量。
不過，目前沒有證據顯示，在11月針對超市發動的網絡攻擊中，家用電器成為了攻擊目標。
英國國家網絡安全中心（NCSC）前行政總裁西亞蘭·馬丁（Ciaran Martin）表示，製造商需要採取更多措施，提升連網設備的安全性。
他說：「我們需要對大型科技公司提出更多要求，讓它們從一開始就為我們提供更安全的設備和產品。」
他建議消費者保持設備更新，並在可行情況下啟用多重身份驗證。
自2024年4月起，英國法律已要求部分消費級智能設備製造商符合最低網絡安全標準，包括密碼管理和安全更新方面的要求。
英國國家網絡安全中心表示，正與國際夥伴及業界合作，以了解這些超市事件的情況，但目前並未發現對英國造成任何影響。
不過，英國網絡防禦（UK Cyber Defence）的研究人員已識別出超過800個與英國零售商相關的製冷及樓宇控制系統介面，可透過公共互聯網存取。
這並不一定意味著它們能夠被入侵，但可能使其暴露於利用弱密碼或軟件漏洞的攻擊者面前。
在早前超市遭受網絡攻擊後，政府已與食品零售業高層舉行會談，討論網絡韌性問題。
英國零售聯盟（British Retail Consortium）行政總裁海倫·狄金森（Helen Dickinson）表示，網絡安全事件是零售商的一大憂慮，各企業正與國家網絡安全中心合作，共享情報並強化防禦能力。
2025年5月，英國超市馬莎百貨（M&S）和合作社集團（Co-op）遭勒索軟件黑客攻擊時，兩家零售商一度難以用新鮮貨品補充部分門店貨架。
網絡安全公司 SentinelOne 研究員湯姆·黑格爾（Tom Hegel）表示，零售商必須更清楚界定責任歸屬。
他說：「零售商需要回答的問題是，誰負責這些設備的安全，而不只是誰負責維修它們。」
他表示，互聯網連接能使日常科技產品更加方便，但安全措施必須同步跟上。
他說：「一旦攻擊者能夠操控這些控制系統，像除霜這樣的正常功能也會變成干擾工具。」
他說：「改變一項設定就可能摧毀實體庫存，而不只是干擾電腦系統。」
在家庭以外，連網技術亦被用於遠程管理工業機械和車輛。
網絡安全專家肯·芒羅（Ken Munro）提到2015年的一次演示，研究人員透過一輛Jeep汽車連接互聯網的娛樂系統進行遠程入侵，促使業界加強車輛安全措施。
他說：「幸運的是，汽車行業已意識到這個問題，並作出了修復。」
流動通訊連接也被廣泛用於監察發電廠及供水網絡中的設備，讓工程師能夠遠程管理系統。
芒羅表示，英國公共事業機構在保護這些連接方面普遍做得不錯，但世界各地的標準並不一致。
他最擔心的是規模較小、資金不足的公用事業公司，這些公司可能仍依賴較舊且存在漏洞的設備。
Zscaler 網絡安全專家奧利維耶·達洛伊（Olivier Daloy）表示，如果缺乏適當的保護措施，任何接入互聯網的「工廠或設備」，從汽車製造商到電力或交通基礎設施，都可能面臨類似風險。
本文原以英文撰寫，我們使用了人工智能協助翻譯，並由BBC記者在發佈前進行審核。了解更多關於我們如何使用人工智能的資訊。

content:
中国国家主席习近平和对中国进行国事访问的阿曼苏丹海赛姆·本·塔里克·阿勒赛义德，在北京人民大会堂出席欢迎仪式。(2026年11月2日)
在美国对伊朗持续进行有限度打击之际，中国高调发动外交行动介入斡旋。北京这个月将派遣特使前往中东，试图推动对话并缓解地区紧张局势。观察人士指出，中国在中东影响力虽有所增长，不过要斡旋止战却是心有余而力不足，充其量只能营造出一个空泛的和平促进者形象。
美国总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)星期二(11月３日)证实，美军星期一晚间对伊朗格什姆岛(Qeshm Island)发动“小规模袭击”。《华尔街日报》援引美国官员的话报道，此次打击是近几周一系列有限度、有针对性的打击行动之一。
美军执行打击前一刻，中国国家主席习近平在北京会晤首次对中国进行国事访问的阿曼苏丹海赛姆·本·塔里克·阿勒赛义德(Haitham Bin Tariq Al-Said)。
据联合声明，阿曼支持习近平先后提出的一系列致力于中东和平稳定的倡议和主张，期待中国为实现中东长治久安发挥更大作用。
声明也提到，双方呼吁坚持通过政治外交途径化解争端，尽早实现全面停火止战，达成包括核问题在内的全面协议；双方认为霍尔木兹海峡应恢复正常、安全通航。
中国外交部发言人毛宁星期一于例行记者会上指出，中国中东问题特使翟雋以及非洲事务特别代表刘显法将于11月上中旬分赴地区国家穿梭访问，旨在“劝和促谈、缓局降温，为维护地区和平稳定发挥建设性作用”。
北京是德黑兰的重要盟友，也是伊朗原油的最大买家。与此同时，中国高度依赖经霍尔木兹海峡运输的能源，长期冲突可能干扰航运及供应链。
《华盛顿邮报》星期三报道称随着中东局势可能进入更危险阶段，中方领导层正试图在决定区域未来走向的过程中取得一席之地，并将自身塑造成维护稳定的力量。
华盛顿智库中东问题研究所中东-亚洲项目主任约翰·卡拉布莱斯(John Calabrese)指出，北京仍沿用惯用策略，也就是呼吁各方保持克制、支持停火并援引国际法，并将自己定位为对话的潜在推动者。
他认为，2023年在中国斡旋下达成的沙乌地阿拉伯-伊朗和解，虽然彰显出北京外交作用的影响力，也揭露了其局限。
卡拉布莱斯通过电邮向美国之音表示：“促进外交对话与成为可信的和平斡旋者之间存在着巨大的鸿沟。”
他解释道，在双方都希望缓和局势的政治背景下，中国所惯用的和解机制或许有效；一旦地区紧张局势从外交层面转向军事对抗，缺乏强制力的斡旋就难以保证。
卡拉布莱斯强调，北京虽然扩大其在中东的影响力，并与各方建立了联系，但它既缺乏足够的筹码，也缺乏承担有效调解所带来的风险和责任的意愿。“作为调解人尚且能力不足，更遑论安全保障者。”
观察人士说，促进和平调解的重要筹码之一是斡旋方本身的军事存在，但是中国既不愿被卷入冲突，在中东也不具备威慑力量，因此对该地区安全保障的能力十分有限。
位于台北的国防安全研究院副研究员黄恩浩指出，中国目前是采“搭便车”策略，也就是由美国海军安全体系来保护国际能源航线。换言之，中国不愿承担区域安全的沉重成本，只有在条件成熟时推一把，其行为趋近于“半调解”。
尽管北京被指控给予伊朗军事上的支持，包括导弹与军工技术转移，以及情报与卫星支援，然而在中东缺乏军事存在是不争事实。
黄恩浩告诉美国之音：“(斡旋)施力会相当有限，因为它(中国)基本上外交政策是不干涉它国内政，再来就是说它在中东地区就是输出一些投资、基础设施甚至是一带一路的一些项目，所以基本上它还是以经贸外交为主，在安全部分，主导的还是美国、以色列。”
美国之音就中国派遣特使前往中东调停一事向美国国务院和白宫发出置评请求，至报道发表前，还未收到回应。
位于台北的政治大学外交学系教授李登科接受美国之音采访时表示，北京是真心希望能够扮演斡旋者的角色。如果斡旋成功不仅提升国际形象，更能确保其经济利益，然而问题在于中国没办法满足美伊双方的条件。
自2月底中东战事爆发以来，历经多轮交火与短暂停火协议破裂。美国坚持霍尔木兹海峡必须立即、无条件开放，并彻底限制伊朗核计划。
伊朗国家安全委员会秘书穆赫辛·雷扎伊(Mohsen Rezaei)星期二重申，美方必须完整、明确回应伊朗提出的7项条件；这些条件包括取消石油制裁、结束美国海上封锁，以及解冻伊朗被冻结的资金。
李登科说：“它(中国)有兴趣介入是一回事，能不能介入又是一回事。那当然表面上美国不会去拒绝，只是说你要美国同意(停火)的话，美国可能要求中国说，你要介入这个斡旋或调解没有问题，但是你一定要让伊朗接受我的条件，那这个(中国)做不到嘛。”
李登科进一步指出，中国不仅没有能力调停美伊之间的战事，就连伊朗与周边阿拉伯国家的冲突，恐怕也是束手无策。
习近平在会晤阿曼苏丹海赛姆时表示，中东和海湾地区不应成为大国竞争的战场，中国愿与阿拉伯国家共同努力，实现持久和平。
包括阿曼在内，沙特阿拉伯、卡达、阿联酋、巴林及科威特等海湾国家，在美伊战争期间皆曾遭伊朗袭击。中国虽然是伊朗坚定盟友，同时也和这些阿拉伯国家保持密切关系。
李登科指出，海湾地区的阿拉伯国家因为有美军基地，所以成为伊朗的打击目标，而这也是伊朗“以战止战”的筹码。从德黑兰政权的角度而言，没道理放着这个杀手锏不用，毕竟中国所能给予的安全保障仍比不上自身的吓阻力。

# Hong Kong activist jailed for 10 more years for collusion with foreign forces

Issued on: 05/11/2026 - 12:29

Share

Hong Kong democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 more years in jail on Thursday for colluding with foreign powers, the second time he has been penalised under the city's national security law. Hong, 30, is one of the most globally recognised faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement and has already spent almost six years behind bars. He is now not due for release until late 2036.

content:
台湾国策研究院星期四（11月5日）举行座谈会，探讨美国期中选后局势与对台影响。图为第一场次座谈，台上左起为台湾中央研究院政治学研究所特聘研究员兼所长吴重礼、中华经济研究院经济法制研究中心主任李淳、主持人国策院执行长王宏仁、国策研究院资深顾问高硕泰及中研院政治所助研究员傅泽民。 （缪宗翰摄）
美国国会席次翻转后，台湾学者认为，民主党掌控两院将加强对特朗普政府的监督，美国挺台方向未必改变，但台湾须经营新一届国会关系，并准备应对贸易协议审查、关税和科技管制变化；分立政府也可能使美国总统特朗普在外交和安全领域采取更强势行动。
美国星期二（11月3日）举行中期选举，民主党赢得众议院和参议院控制权。参议院至少54席归民主党阵营、44席由共和党取得；众议院民主党已确保过半，至少赢得237席，共和党139席。民主党翻转至少七个参院席位，众院净增逾20席。
州长选举方面，民主党翻转阿拉斯加、乔治亚、爱荷华、内华达、俄亥俄和得州六州，预计将以29比20掌握州长职位多数；堪萨斯州长选举仍未决。
台湾国策研究院星期四（11月5日）在台北举行座谈会，邀请学者分析这次选举对美国国会外交、经贸科技政策及台海安全等影响。
国策研究院资深顾问高硕泰在会中分析，这次大选后，民主党将运用监督、听证、任​​命和预算等权力牵制白宫。
他形容这场选举是“一股蓝色的洋流变成了蓝色的海啸”，并说特朗普虽称接受结果，却“没有认输”，因为“他（特朗普）的字典里面没有‘妥协’这两个字”。高硕泰认为，特朗普在国内受制后，可能转而在外交和国安政策上展现强势，以证明自己并非“跛鸭”。
高硕泰曾于2016年6月至2020年7月担任台湾驻美国代表。他指出，台湾长年发展与美国国会议员关系，历来参众两院都有约三分之一的议员参与台湾连线。但这次大选后，参院台湾连线30人中有八人将离任，众院也有近30人离开，台湾应尽早盘点并争取新支持者。
另外，高硕泰也提醒，近年美国国会议员访台人数和次数下滑，部分议员因北京在时任众院议长佩洛西访台后举行军演，以及特朗普对台言论、对北京示好而却步。
他呼吁台湾政府重新锁定邀访对象、把握州政府交流机会，并强调台美关系“不可断、不能断、也不会断”，台湾须冷静务实，避免一厢情愿。
曾任台湾驻欧盟兼驻比利时代表的中华经济研究院经济法制研究中心主任李淳则判断，民主党胜选不会使美国关税和科技政策“发生逆转”，但国会参与将大幅提升。
他说，民主党可能挑战特朗普对加拿大、墨西哥及其他伙伴加征关税的做法；对华战略竞争则有跨党派共识，特别是对华科技管制“力道与强度不会下降”，美国国会将推动更制度化、可检验的管制依据。
李淳进一步指出，美国推动再工业化的目标不变，政策工具可能由限制转向更多补贴和奖励。台美贸易协议未必因此被推翻，但国会可能要求更大审查空间，并修法限制总统单方面加征关税。台湾对美经贸、投资和科技合作料将延续，但须因应政策工具与适用对象变化。
对于美国中期选举对台海安全的影响，台湾国安局外围智库亚太和平研究基金会执行长董立文认为，关键仍在中美战略竞争的结构性限制，因此影响有限。
台湾国策研究院11月5日举行座谈会，探讨美国期中选后局势与对台影响。图片左起为座谈会第二场次主持人、国策院副院长郭育仁，亚太和平研究基金会执行长董立文，台湾师范大学东亚学系教授范世平。（缪宗翰摄）
董立文以2018年和2022年美国中期选举为例说，分立政府虽造成内政僵局，却未削弱国会对华强硬共识及跨党派挺台力量。
他因此判断，这次选后美国国会将加强监督白宫对华谈判、关税和军售；即使白宫寻求有限缓和，台湾作为对华交易筹码的空间也越来越小。

content:
时任“香港众志”秘书长的黄之锋2019年9月17日抵达华盛顿国会山，就香港的民主运动向美国国会及行政当局中国委员会作证。他和其他香港民主派人士在听证会上呼吁美国国会尽快通过《香港人权与民主法案》，以向北京和香港特区政府施压。 （法新社）
正在为香港民主派“35+初选案”服刑的前香港众志秘书长黄之锋，星期四（11月5日）因串谋勾结外国势力危害国家安全罪，被香港高等法院判处监禁10年，预计要到2036年才能获释。
控罪指黄之锋于2020年7月1日至11月23日期间，与已流亡英国的前香港众志主席罗冠聪及其他身份不详人士串谋，请求外国或境外机构、组织和人员，对中国中央政府或香港特区政府实施制裁、封锁或其他敌对行动。
《香港国安法》指定法官谭耀豪星期四宣读判词时指出，案发时，香港正面对社会动荡及暴动所带来的严重影响，在国家安全及法治方面承受极高风险。在这关键时刻，被告与联系人继续一同串谋，与外国主要或高级官员或境外势力直接会晤，公然呼吁他们对中国、香港及官员实施制裁、封锁或其他敌对措施，还透过自己的社交媒体账户、西方主流新闻媒体或机构作出类似呼吁。
法官认为，被告与罗冠聪两人是本案的主谋，可以被视为最前沿的倡议者，惩罚必须与罪行的严重性相称，也要表达对有关计划及行为的厌恶，以达到阻吓效果。
法官指出，基于被告认罪及求情，法庭将量刑起点下调三年，判处被告入狱10年，即《香港国安法》第二十九条下“罪行重大”所须判处的最低刑期，其中两个月又两天与被告目前服刑案件的刑期同期执行，即黄之锋需加监九年10个月。黄之锋原定明年1月刑满释放，现在预计要2036年11月才刑满，出狱时或已年届40岁。
法官用了一个半小时读毕全份判辞，包括详述案情，全程都要黄之锋站立。他不时用手撑着围栏，闻判10年后皱眉。有旁听人士散庭后相拥而哭。
上个月刚满30岁的黄之锋，是香港2014年“占领运动”和2019年反修例运动的知名人物。这是他第二次因违反《香港国安法》被判刑，也是《香港国安法》实施以来，再有知名民主派人士因勾结外国势力罪被判处长期监禁。黄之锋自2020年底起已因不同案件入狱，至今身在狱中超过六年。
港府发言人对法庭的判决表示欢迎，指对黄之锋予以重判，彻底打破危害国家安全分子披着所谓“国际线”或“国际倡议”外衣便能逃避法律追责的幻想，向国际社会表明香港特区维护国家安全的坚定决心。“这次判刑显示法庭确定本案涉及外国势力，案情严重，需要判处具阻吓性的刑期。此外，特区政府会依法充公黄之锋的罪行相关财产。”
美国驻香港总领事馆强烈谴责香港高等法院对民主活动人士黄之锋追加10年监禁的判决，并呼吁立即释放他。
发言人说：“黄之锋自2020年12月以来一直被不公正地监禁，这表明北京不惜采取极端手段，也要让那些在香港倡导基本自由的人噤声。”
台湾陆委会同日发表声明，对黄之锋判刑表示强烈谴责与忧心，并称中共及港府应停止对民主人士的打压与司法迫害，保障港人应有的基本人权与言论自由。
香港中文大学政务与政策科学学院讲师孔永乐接受《联合早报》访问时说，黄之锋在国际社会有相当大的知名度，过往在促请外国对香港特区实施制裁或其他敌对行动上的态度明确且积极。然而，香港法院考量到他及早认罪，且于服刑期间更生表现良好，最终判处他有期徒刑10年，“法理与量刑上都属于合理的决定”。
孔永乐认为，从政治的角度来看，10年是一个漫长的周期，10年后的香港年轻一代对黄之锋是否还维持深刻的认知让人存疑，黄之锋未来能延续的影响力恐怕将很有限。
曾在黎智英案中担任控方证人的香港《苹果日报》前社长张剑虹、重光团队成员陈梓华与李宇轩等涉国安案件犯人，据报早前提前获释。孔永乐认为，这有可能影响目前在押的一些民主派人士，促使他们转变对中国大陆的政治立场。

# 北京未批准大规模进口 约60万枚英伟达H200芯片被指滞留香港

据路透社援引两位知情人士报导称，约有60万枚英伟达先进人工智能芯片目前存放在香港，等待运往中国内地。尽管中国科技企业有相关需求，但北京方面尚未批准这些芯片的大规模进口。

发表时间： 05/11/2026 - 13:22 更改时间： 05/11/2026 - 13:25

 7 分钟 浏览时间

 英伟达标志和中国国旗示意图 © 路透社图片

 作者： [弗林](https://www.rfi.fr/cn/%E4%BD%9C%E8%80%85/%E5%BC%97%E6%9E%97/ "弗林")

广告

继续浏览后续

报导指，这批此前未被披露的H200芯片库存，反映出北京方面不愿进一步增加对美国技术的依赖。与此同时，中国企业又迫切需要英伟达的先进算力，以满足中国这一全球第二大经济体中激增的人工智能需求。

三位知情人士称，近几个月来，中方已允许部分这些芯片进入国内。其中一位知情人士称，过去几个月里，中国多家大型互联网公司各自获得了约1万枚H200芯片。

三位知情人士表示，这些芯片是通过中间商和间接渠道以少量方式运入的，但未明确具体数量。不过，这些人士称，北京方面尚未批准大规模的芯片进口至中国内地。

中国工信部和国家发展改革委未回应置评请求。英伟达以及中国的科技巨头——阿里巴巴、字节跳动、深度求索（DeepSeek）和腾讯——也均未作出回应。

H200并非英伟达最新款的人工智能处理器，但它所具备的能力是目前中国国产替代产品尚无法比拟的。这使得它在训练人工智能模型时非常有用，尤其是在与英伟达的软件配套使用时。

自2022年以来，美国政府实施的出口管制旨在限制中国获取英伟达的先进芯片以及制造这些芯片所需的设备。由于合规供应渠道受限，中国买家转而寻求中间商或通过间接途径进行采购，这推高了非官方市场上的价格。

据一位知情人士透露，截至10月底，在中国内地，一台搭载8枚H200芯片的服务器售价超过600万元人民币，约为一年前价格的三倍。该人士还指出，搭载英伟达更新款、受到美国出口管制限制的Blackwell芯片的服务器，单台报价则超过了2000万元人民币。

上述H200芯片卷入了华盛顿与北京之间更广泛的贸易与技术博弈之中。美方曾一度禁止向中国出口H200芯片；但在去年，特朗普政府允许英伟达将该芯片出售给经批准的中国客户。这一政策转变发生在美中贸易谈判之后。

与此同时，中国当局也针对H200的进口实施了限制措施，这反映出其对依赖美国技术的担忧。

美国科技媒体《信息报》7月报导称，中国官方已告知包括阿里巴巴、字节跳动和深度求索在内的多家企业，它们或可获准购买数量有限的H200芯片，用于人工智能模型的训练。

报导称，获批芯片总量可能不到20万枚；此外，北京方面希望这些企业在进行人工智能推理——即运行人工智能模型任务时，优先选用中国国产处理器。

路透社上月报导称，字节跳动、阿里巴巴和腾讯已订购了超过300万张英伟达RTX Pro 5500显卡——这是一款性能较弱、符合出口管制要求的产品——其总标价超过350亿美元。

资料照片：香港民主派人士黄之锋(左)和周庭在香港因涉嫌组织非法抗议被捕后，乘警车抵达东区法院。(2019年8月30日)
香港高等法院星期四(11月5日)依据《香港国安法》，以串谋勾结外国势力罪向民主派活动人士黄之锋加判10年监禁。现年30岁的黄之锋已被关押近六年，原定于2027年1月获释，如今预计要到2036年底才能出狱。
法院以13年监禁为量刑起点，因黄之锋认罪而减刑至10年。检方指控他与流亡海外的民主派人士罗冠聪等人串谋，寻求外国对香港及中国实施制裁。
美国驻香港及澳门总领事馆当天发表声明，强烈谴责这一判决，并要求立即释放黄之锋。发言人向法新社表示，黄之锋自2020年12月以来一直遭到不公正监禁，判决表明北京“不惜采取极端手段，让那些在香港倡导基本自由的人士噤声”。
美国国会众议院中国问题特设委员会主席，来自密歇根州的共和党联邦众议员约翰·穆勒纳尔(John Moolenaar)发表声明，谴责中国当局的“无耻表现”。
“黄之锋是一个敢于对抗威权超级大国的英雄。他之所以对毫无根据的外国勾结罪名认罪，是因为中共系统性地侵蚀了香港的司法独立。”
穆勒纳尔继续指出，中共实际上用压制性的《国家安全法》对黄之锋进行了判决。“这是中共完全无视造物主赋予所有人的生命和自由等普世人权的无耻表现。黄之锋和香港现在比以往任何时候都更需要国际社会的支持。他应该立即获释，与他的家人团聚。”穆勒纳尔在声明中说。
英国国会保守党议员汤姆·图根达特(Tom Tugendhat)在X上发帖呼吁各界想想黄之锋和他的勇气。
“今天花点时间想想黄之锋的勇气。一个年轻的活动人士，他唯一的‘罪行’就是为香港人的自由辩护。今天，因为他的勇气，他被中国共产党判了十年监禁。他本可以逃跑，本可以流亡海外，但他选择了勇敢。”图根达特写道。
台湾陆委会副主委梁文杰对香港法院的判决表示“谴责和痛心”。梁文杰说，等黄之锋10年后服刑期满出狱时，已经年满40岁。一个人从24岁一路遭到关押，直到40岁才重获自由，所承受的人生影响难以想象。
梁文杰呼吁中共和港府停止对民主派人士的打压和司法迫害，终止以国家安全为名的政治滥诉，保障港人拥有的基本人权与言论自由。
许多国际人权组织也谴责这一判决。北京则表示支持香港依法打击危害国家安全的行为。
法新社报道，星期四在香港高等法庭外的香港民众对判决结果表示“震惊”和“悲伤”。
一位女士说，“从我个人的角度来看，这令人震惊。这让我们对长期以来的司法制度产生质疑。对于人权和普世原则应当如何确立，国际社会理应存在共识。过去法律允许的一些活动，如今却变成违法行为，这是不合理的。类似这样不公正的定罪实在太多了。”
香港前民间人权阵线召集人陈皓桓对法新社说，判决很重令他非常难过。
“我当然感到难过，也为他感到惋惜。但眼下，我们什么也做不了。我们真的没有其他选择，只能彼此支持、互相鼓励。”他说。
黄之锋对“串谋勾结外国势力危害国家安全”指控当庭认罪；美国议员和人权组织强烈谴责政治迫害
穆勒纳尔致函特朗普总统与卢比奥国务卿，呼吁促释中国良心犯并制裁涉黎智英案香港官员
香港“47人案”12名被告上诉全被驳回，人权组织称当局“错失纠正不公义判决的机会”

summary: 前联邦参议员、民主党人谢罗德·布朗(Sherrod Brown)在今年的中期选举击败了他的共和党籍对手，明年1月将重返参议院。 曾任美国国会及行政当局中国委员会(Congressional-Executive Commission on China，CECC)主席的前联邦参议员、民主党人谢罗德·布朗(Sherrod Brown)在星期二(11月3日)的中期选举中获胜。他在俄亥俄州的参议员选战中击败了共和党对手乔恩·赫斯特德(Jon Husted)，将于明年1月宣誓就职。 布朗
content:
前联邦参议员、民主党人谢罗德·布朗(Sherrod Brown)在今年的中期选举击败了他的共和党籍对手，明年1月将重返参议院。
曾任美国国会及行政当局中国委员会(Congressional-Executive Commission on China，CECC)主席的前联邦参议员、民主党人谢罗德·布朗(Sherrod Brown)在星期二(11月3日)的中期选举中获胜。他在俄亥俄州的参议员选战中击败了共和党对手乔恩·赫斯特德(Jon Husted)，将于明年1月宣誓就职。
布朗长期关注中国和台湾事务。他在担任联邦众议员时，共同创立了众议院台湾连线。之后，在上次担任参议员时，他曾是参议院台湾连线成员。布朗还曾长期担任CECC的委员，并先后出任该委员会的共同主席与主席。
2024年败选的布朗如今又将重返参议院。美国之音(VOA)总结了他之前在有关中国和台湾议题上的公开立场和言论。
布朗从2007年至2025年担任参议员，长期关注中国人权和宗教自由问题，他支持制裁参与香港镇压者，并把中国对维吾尔人的大规模监控列为出口管制理由。
在贸易方面，布朗长期支持针对中国的“301条款”(Section 301)关税，要求阻止中国电动汽车进入美国。
在科技方面，布朗推动立法，支持先进芯片及半导体设备出口管制、审查美国对华超级智能、量子和芯片投资，避免用于中国国防发展。
布朗在推出《出境投资透明法》(Outbound Investment Transparency Act)时的新闻稿中说：“美国的资金和专业知识不应用于增强中国政府的军事和情报能力。在我们推动《出境投资透明法》成为法律的同时，行政当局必须迅速执行该命令，确保美国企业投资不会帮助中国开发将被用来对付我们的技术。”
在台湾问题上，他支持《台湾关系法》、“六项保证”及向台湾出售F-16战机，并认为台湾未来应由台湾人民决定，同时维持美国“不支持台湾独立”的政策框架；他在2024年支持台湾和印太援助。
在星期二另一场关键的参议员选战中，民主党人克里斯·帕帕斯(Chris Pappas)在新罕布什尔州战胜了共和党对手约翰·苏努努(John Sununu)。帕帕斯现任联邦众议员，也在中国和台湾议题上表达了鲜明立场。
帕帕斯在他的竞选网站上将中国与俄罗斯、伊朗并列为威权竞争者，主张依靠盟友、保护民主及维持美国的利益和价值观。
在贸易方面，他在2025年反对普遍、无差别关税，特别点名当时对中国商品高达145%的税率，认为成本先由美国进口商承担，最终转嫁消费者。
在对台湾问题上，他多次强调美国应加强与“民主盟友”台湾的外交伙伴关系，并反制中国“恐吓与霸凌台湾”。
帕帕斯是众议院台湾连线成员。他曾在2025年6月参与重新推出《台湾代表处法案》(Taiwan Representative Office Act)。这部由两院两党议员推出的法案要求将“驻美国台北经济文化代表处”正式更名为“台湾代表处”。
帕帕斯在谈到这项提案时说：“随着台湾面临日益严峻的安全和主权威胁，我们必须继续加强与民主盟友的外交伙伴关系。这项两党法案将对台湾事实上的大使馆予以恰当承认，以展示我们的持续支持。我们必须继续与民主盟友站在一起，反对威权政权，并反击中国恐吓与霸凌台湾和其他国家的企图。”
在美中科技竞争方面，他支持《芯片与科学法案》(CHIPS and Science Act)，称将半导体生产带回美国并帮助美国“胜过中国”。
在人权方面，他参与推出《阻止中共法》(STOP CCP Act)，称中共必须为国家支持的针对维吾尔族穆斯林的种族灭绝及长期人权侵害负责；该法案针对涉及新疆镇压、香港自治受损和对台胁迫的中共高层实施金融和签证制裁。

title: The Pentagon needs more ammo for the Iran war. Small communities are paying the price.
zh_title: 五角大楼需要更多弹药来应对伊朗战争。小社区正在付出代价。
summary: 编者注：本文首次发表于《战马》，这是一家屡获殊荣的非营利新闻机构，旨在教育公众服兵役。订阅他们的时事通讯。 2024 年秋天，飓风海伦席卷东海岸，新河的水淹没了城镇，摧毁了西弗吉尼亚州、北卡罗来纳州和弗吉尼亚州部分地区的桥梁。在弗吉尼亚州雷德福，洪水最高达到 31 英尺。就在下游，河水涌入雷德福德陆军弹药厂，冲破了仓库大门，冲毁了十几个装有数千名弹药的储存容器。
content:
编者注：本文首次发表于《战马》，这是一家屡获殊荣的非营利新闻机构，旨在教育公众服兵役。订阅他们的时事通讯。 2024 年秋天，飓风海伦席卷东海岸，新河的水淹没了城镇，摧毁了西弗吉尼亚州、北卡罗来纳州和弗吉尼亚州部分地区的桥梁。在弗吉尼亚州雷德福，洪水最高达到 31 英尺。就在下游，河流涌入雷德福德陆军弹药厂，冲破仓库大门，冲走了十几个装有数千加仑有毒化学品的储存容器。直到几周后，陆军才向居民发出关于装满邻苯二甲酸二丁酯的集装箱的警告，邻苯二甲酸二丁酯是火箭推进剂的关键成分，与人类癌症和生殖问题有关，还有数百加仑柴油和超过10万磅被硫酸钙污染的废水，这些集装箱已在洪水中被冲走。官员们后来表示，他们假设这些集装箱会沉入河底，洪水会稀释任何化学品泄漏。然而，至少有一个集装箱被冲到附近的土地上，部分集装箱已被排干。据弗吉尼亚州环境质量部称，两年后，三人仍下落不明，该部门发现超过 1,500 加仑的液体已泄漏到环境中。
雷德福陆军弹药厂早在 2024 年就因向新河排放超标污染物而被点名。它在 2023 年也面临着类似的处罚。2022 年，弗吉尼亚州环境监管机构将雷德福列为该州最大的毒素排放者。 “他们经常被指责向水中添加过量的铅，或向空气中释放其他有毒物质，或者燃烧比预期更多的化学物质，”阿森纳责任公民组织的创始人艾莉莎·卡彭特说，该组织倡导在雷德福德采取更严格的环保措施。雷德福德也是国家军火供应链的重要组成部分：它是火炮和火箭所用某些类型推进剂的唯一国内生产商。当五角大楼采取行动补充其耗尽的弹药库存并增加产量时，它在一定程度上依赖于雷德福等老化的陆军弹药工厂网络，其中一些工厂有着长期违反环境和安全法规的历史。一名工人在雷德福陆军弹药厂检查火箭筒推进剂。 （多丽丝·惠普尔摄，雷德福德陆军弹药厂提供）支持者表示，军方经常将这些风险视为生产的次要风险，让工人和附近社区承担后果。
“国防部机构的记录并不好，”在奥巴马政府期间帮助监督环境保护局有毒物质清理工作的马西·斯坦尼斯劳斯说，“始终是防御。‘这是我们的使命。’其他一切都是次要的。”现在，支持者担心生产更多弹药的压力可能会加剧当地社区面临的风险。他们认为，重建美国军火库的成本不成比例地由工厂工人和设施周围的大多数农村社区承担。卡彭特说：“这对军队来说很便宜，但对我们、对我们的一生来说却非常昂贵。” “如果不增加该产品产生的有毒副产品，就无法增加产量
